prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and the optical lattice clock fifth, so this is a real move on my part. Reading the other seven ballots, the clock is the one candidate where scientific, attribution and maturity arguments all line up. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a specific, original invention. Ye's group carried it to the 1e-18 level and into many-body clock physics. The result has been reproduced by several independent laboratories, and the international discussion on redefining the second shows it has become infrastructure for measurement. The two-name credit is also the cleanest on the shortlist: every colleague who ranked B009 proposed exactly Katori and Ye. That leaves room for the unresolved credit problems in other candidates to be settled without forcing this one. My own temperament is to look for what nature delivers, and the clock is increasingly a tool for asking nature questions (variation of constants, dark-matter couplings, relativistic geodesy), not merely a better instrument.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is the one I would have pressed against it in my opening ballot: it is an invention in metrology, and the committee has already honoured the frequency-comb lineage (2005) and ion control (2012). If the prize is read as a precision-engineering award, it sits less comfortably with the discovery criterion than IceCube's observation of a new astrophysical messenger or the topological-insulator work, which changed how we classify phases of matter. Eight members ranking it, six in the top three, also shows it is the safe consensus pick, and I do not want to mistake breadth of agreement for depth of scientific weight. The clocks have not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of their own; their promise is still largely prospective.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B009 first as exactly the measurement physics whose reach is set by what can be measured, with Katori the decisive conceptual inventor and Ye the implementer of the 1e-18 systematic frontier, and with other groups contributing demonstrations but not the founding idea.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and I think it is the strongest part of the case: the founding idea and the record-setting realization sit with two people, which is rare. Where I would qualify Kroll is on the claim that no sign of fragility remains. The comb and ion-clock lineage means the committee must be able to phrase a citation that clearly differs from 2005 and 2012, so I have written the citation around the lattice-clock invention itself and not clocks in general. I also note Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory connection through Ye; that does not seem disqualifying to me, but the chair may want it noted when this candidate is discussed.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first, as a detector-driven opening of a new observational window, but argues the decisive pair is Halzen and Karle, with Spiering's role important but less central, and wants to know whether to anchor on the diffuse-flux discovery or wait for firmer source identification.
responses.response: We start from the same place on B052, and I take the attribution point seriously: my own three-name proposal (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) is probably the weakest part of my opening case, given that the wider lineage through AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND is outside the credited names. On timing I disagree with the suggestion of waiting. The diffuse flux is established and independently confirmed, so I would not hold the discovery hostage to the source associations. But I now think B052 needs more committee discussion of who is credited before I can place it above the clock. Only three of us ranked it, and Olsson placed it seventh, so I cannot treat my first place as a mandate. I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron optics first as a clear invention with wide impact and a natural Rose, Haider, Urban triple, and ranks IceCube seventh because credit inside a several-hundred-person collaboration is hard to divide fairly and the origin of most of the flux is unresolved.
responses.response: Her IceCube objection is a fair one and I have taken it on board: the unsettled origin of most of the neutrino flux is a real interpretive gap, even if the discovery of the flux itself is not in doubt. On B017 I respectfully disagree in emphasis. The corrector is a beautiful and mature enabling technology, but only she and Eriksson (who put it eighth) ranked it, and I would want a discovery-level rationale beyond the instrument, as Eriksson also points out. The same worry applies to the clock, and I do not exempt B009 from it. The difference I see is that clocks directly turn into tests of fundamental physics, whereas the microscope's primary impact is across materials and chemistry.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B009 first and B018 second, treats Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a coherent theory-plus-experiment prize despite the Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and 3D omissions, and notes that the 2016 topological-phases prize left this area open.
responses.response: I share her second place and, on balance, I think B018 is the strongest competitor to the clock. Where I want to push is her suggestion that the BHZ omission is manageable. Molenkamp's HgTe experiment followed a proposal by theorists who are not on the supplied list, so a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp prize leaves a genuine fairness problem that the committee, not the nomination, would have to answer. Because the credited-name limit is three, I cannot repair this by adding names. That is why I put B018 as an alternative and not as my preferred configuration, despite ranking it second.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, openly flagging field and Chalmers proximity, and argues that it is distinct from the 2025 circuit prize, with Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf as the decisive three even though Wallraff's role is uncovered.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about proximity, and I agree that circuit QED is scientifically distinct from the macroscopic tunnelling work honoured in 2025. My concern is timing and balance, not merit: a second superconducting-circuit prize right after 2025 would be a hard sell, and the missing Wallraff credit adds to the attribution problem. Only four members ranked B008 and it did not reach the top three for anyone except Johansson, so I do not support making it the centre of the prize this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a metrology invention as discovery-level physics so soon after the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether the credited-name limit of three prevents a fair B018 prize because the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal falls outside the supplied names.
How to divide credit for IceCube among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors if the committee wants an astroparticle prize.
I have not independently verified the history of lattice-clock priority or accuracy milestones; my judgement rests on the opening ballots and my general knowledge as a theorist outside this subfield.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are in string theory and cosmology and have no link to any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I do note, as a matter of procedure, that Kroll has disclosed a research period in Hall's laboratory and that Johansson has flagged institutional proximity to circuit QED.
